rows.text: Remove Graph metadata checks per cache block from the validated read-session fast path; implement and measure shared session setup, bounded sequential windows and safe renewal as specified in [read-session efficiency](adr/0004-read-session-efficiency.md).
rows.evidence: docs/validation.md#the-same-file-through-two-cold-mounts-with-the-path-off-and-on plus #read-session-behaviour-on-a-live-mount, benchmarks/mount-level-read-bytes.json and live-read-session-counters.json, live 2026-09-09. All four clauses are now evidenced on a live mount. Per-cache-block metadata checks: conservative Graph metadata GETs track content GETs at about two per block (22 against 10, and 7 against 3 at a four-fold smaller size) while the optimized path does not (4 against 4, 3 against 2), each arm on its own cold engine directory with counters sampled around the read alone. Bytes are SHA-256 identical through the kernel mount at both sizes, with the optimized arm asserted to have bound a session and the conservative arm asserted not to. Shared setup and bounded windows: setups 1 and conditional_windows 3 on a live mount. Safe renewal: renewals 1 under continuous reading across the 60 s lease; an idle pause does not reach it because the read after it is served outside the session. NOT TICKED, and not for want of evidence: conditional_reads is false by default, so a shipped daemon still performs the per-block checks measured absent here. Enabling it is a product decision. CLOSED 2026-09-10: the one thing left was never a measurement. The default was false, so a shipped daemon still made the per-block checks these runs measured absent. The owner made that call on this evidence and conditional_reads is now true in OneDrive::new.

rows.text: Push-triggered metadata updates, reconnection/catch-up and periodic recovery checks, with provider delivery and local reaction latency measured separately.
rows.evidence: docs/validation.md#push-notifications and #subscription-renewal-at-the-real-boundary -- live 2026-09-09: delivery 30.0-32.7 s across eleven samples, local reaction 169-287 ms, measured separately as the box requires. One subscription held 2,999,973 ms, renewed, reconnected, and delivered a fresh change 30,441 ms later. One notification in eleven was never delivered (90 s deadline); the pre-registered interference hypothesis was refuted by an immediately passing retry and the miss stands unexplained; the shipped 30 s poll bounds the impact. Catch-up and periodic recovery are now covered live too (docs/validation.md#catch-up-after-a-reconnection-and-the-periodic-recovery-refresh, benchmarks/live-catchup-and-recovery.json, 2026-09-09): a change made with nothing connected and the poll an hour away was fetched 408 ms after the subscription connected and listed 206 ms later; with no subscription at all the 30 s poll found one in 29,421 ms. Each phase disabled the other and counted zero directory listings before its delta, so neither is explained by activity revalidation. RENEWAL OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-11: the validator held a real Socket.IO subscription for its full lifetime, Microsoft renewed it, and a change made afterwards was delivered through the renewed connection -- 'Renewed subscription connected; checking a new change through it' followed by a passing delivery. That is a renewal the provider performed rather than one a fixture simulated. STILL OPEN: the one notification in eleven that was never delivered remains unexplained; the periodic figure bounds its impact rather than accounting for it. REPLICATED 2026-09-10 on a separate write-grant validation connection, a different day and build. Catch-up: delta 1536 ms after the subscription connected against 408 ms first time, entry listed 206 ms later -- the same figure to the millisecond. Periodic recovery: delta 29,454 ms against 29,421, a difference of 33 ms across two independent runs. Directory freshness through a real mount: three rounds at 5,147 / 5,297 / 5,103 ms total from change to visible, which is the five-second activity revalidation interval and not push. A mounted view following remote changes: create visible in 2 ms, move in 4,650 ms, delete in 4,450 ms.

rows.text: Crash/fault tests at every durable transition and concurrent remote edits.
rows.evidence: docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-crash-coverage.json and durable-transition-sites.json for process death: all 31 runtime durable transitions are crossed by a process that then dies, measured rather than read. 2026-09-11, faults below the process: docs/benchmarks/journal-under-io-faults.json. A dm-flakey device switched to error_writes at runtime and back. What was durable before the fault survives it and reads back byte for byte afterwards; new work is refused as JournalError::Storage rather than as corruption -- reporting a refusing device as a corrupt journal would send a user to recovery steps that destroy work the device still holds. A prediction failed usefully: the journal cannot be OPENED on a failing device, because opening opens SQLite and SQLite writes. So its contents are inaccessible during a fault, which is not the same as lost, and the run makes only the second claim. STILL OPEN: a lying fsync and torn writes are separate injections not yet run, and a true power cut cannot be scripted at all -- it needs someone at the wall socket or a machine with a controllable PSU. That clause is why this box is not ticked.
rows.asserted_by: All 31 runtime durable transitions are crossed by a process that then dies, measured rather than read: each site records itself and each crash fixture persists what it reached. 30 are evidenced in a killed child; the preparation recovery in the process that opens the journal afterwards, because that is where recovery runs. See docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-sites.json. a_journal_on_a_failing_device_refuses_without_losing_what_was_durable runs in three phases against one dm-flakey device in CI; re-run with the sealed payload deliberately overwritten, its recover phase fails.

rows.text: Persistent per-file and recursive-folder pinning with storage reservations.
rows.evidence:
Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. State as of 2026-09-10, rewritten because appending had left resolved 'STILL OPEN' clauses standing in front of the text that resolved them.
COVERED: pins live in the metadata index at schema 7 and survive restart; a reservation is checked against the budget when the pin is made, so a request that will not fit is refused rather than accepted and later evicted; reservations may not claim the whole budget. Reachable from a terminal since 2026-09-10: cirrove pin goes over the control socket to the running daemon, which resolves --path -- including through a shortcut into a linked collection, where a caller outside the daemon recorded the pin under the wrong scope -- and calls materialise_pin or pin_folder. Before that the engine's acting API had no caller outside its own tests and a pin kept nothing. See docs/benchmarks/offline-pinning-reachability.json, which also records the reservation error its own discriminator found: reservations were made in logical bytes while the cache stores a SHA-256 per block, and because pinned blocks are protected the shortfall was never recovered.
MEASURED ON A REAL ACCOUNT 2026-09-11: docs/benchmarks/live-offline-pinning.json. A generated 9,000,000-byte file on the user's business drive, pinned through the same request path the command line uses, reported 9,000,096 bytes resident across three blocks -- the file plus three block digests, which is the reservation correction made the day before arriving at the right answer on a real drive. After the engine was rebuilt and mounted it read back byte for byte with ZERO provider content requests, while an unpinned control in the same folder needed one. This covers the PER-FILE half of the row. STILL OPEN: recursive folder pinning is covered by fixtures only -- real_a_recursive_pin_keeps_the_files_under_a_folder_readable_offline -- and has never run against a real drive, where a subtree can be partly unindexed and can cross into a linked collection.
rows.asserted_by: Persistence: store::pins::tests::a_pin_and_its_protected_blocks_survive_reopening_the_store, and engine::pinning::a_restart_republishes_pins_before_anything_can_evict, which is the stronger of the two because it asserts the ordering rather than only the survival. Recursive folders: engine::pinning::a_folder_pin_covers_every_file_under_it_and_says_what_it_could_not_see and an_unindexed_subtree_is_reported_rather_than_quietly_excluded. Reservations: store::pins::tests::raising_a_pin_counts_only_the_difference_against_the_budget, engine::pinning::a_refused_pin_changes_nothing, content::tests::a_reservation_shrinks_the_budget_the_ordinary_cache_may_fill, and engine::pinning::materialising_a_pin_fetches_its_blocks_and_protects_exactly_those. tests/read_only.rs::a_pin_from_the_command_line_reaches_the_daemon_and_keeps_the_bytes drives a manager, a control socket and the same client function the CLI calls; against the previous source it does not compile. real_a_recursive_pin_keeps_the_files_under_a_folder_readable_offline covers the recursive half through a kernel mount. real_pin_protection_survives_a_restart_and_immediate_cache_pressure covers persistence through Engine::new, a mount and pressure with no pause; two mechanisms establish the protection and either suffices, so it asserts the property rather than which path provides it -- disabling both is what makes it fail. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning is the live check; it is a validator rather than a test, so it asserts on a real account and is not run by CI.

rows.text: Clear unpin/free-space behavior and accurate availability status.
rows.evidence:
Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. State as of 2026-09-10, rewritten for the same reason.
COVERED: availability separates what a pin reserved from what it has actually kept, counted from files present in the cache directory rather than from the block index, which is derived state. Unpin is reachable from a terminal and its effect is asserted -- though not the effect first claimed: releasing a reservation raises the ordinary cache budget, so it frees no bytes and correctly leaves the cache as full as it was; what it changes is protection. A refusal reaches the caller with the numbers and the remedy.
STILL OPEN: behaviour as the budget fills over time and an explanation of it in words rather than JSON; no measured evidence on a real account for this row's own clauses. The live pinning run of 2026-09-11 covers pinning and offline reading, not the budget-filling, cleanup or disk-full behaviour these rows ask about.
rows.asserted_by: engine::pinning::unpinning_releases_the_budget_at_the_cache and store::pins::tests::unpinning_releases_both_the_reservation_and_the_protection cover the free-space half; engine::pinning::availability_separates_what_a_pin_reserved_from_what_it_kept covers the status half. real_unpinned_blocks_stop_being_protected_from_eviction applies the same cache pressure twice, with the pin in force and after it is released, and asserts the blocks survive the first and not the second. real_a_refused_pin_names_the_budget_and_leaves_the_kept_one_alone asserts the refusal names an action, records no pin, disturbs no existing reservation, and leaves the accepted pin readable offline -- the accepted-first assertion is what stops a path that refuses everything from passing.

Reading: a pinned file reads with the provider returning Unavailable and still reads after the engine is rebuilt on the same directory, where the memory cache is empty so the bytes can only come from disk; through a real mount, real_a_pinned_file_reads_offline_through_the_mount_and_an_unpinned_one_does_not asserts the provider read counter did not move and reads an unpinned control that must fail. rows.text: Unsent changes excluded from cache eviction and connection cleanup.
rows.evidence:
Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. State as of 2026-09-10, rewritten for the same reason.
COVERED: eviction only ever removes files whose names it recognises as its own block keys plus its own temporaries, so an unsent journal beside the cache is structurally out of reach, and that is asserted rather than argued. The disable half is asserted through a writable mount. Removal now exists: accounts::forget refuses while the account is enabled, refuses while the journal holds unsent records -- naming how many -- and moves the account directory to removed/ rather than deleting it. Building it was necessary before the clause could be tested at all: with no removal path, a test would have asserted that a thing which does not exist does not delete a journal.
STILL OPEN: no measured evidence on a real account for this row's own clauses. The live pinning run of 2026-09-11 covers pinning and offline reading, not the budget-filling, cleanup or disk-full behaviour these rows ask about.
rows.asserted_by: content::tests::eviction_never_reaches_outside_its_own_block_names, which places an unsent journal entry beside the cache and a non-block file inside it, drives both deletion passes -- evict and the reconcile that runs on reopening -- and asserts a real block was removed as well, so a pass that deleted nothing could not satisfy it. content::tests::eviction_leaves_a_protected_block_and_takes_the_next_one_instead and the_reconcile_pass_at_mount_time_also_leaves_protected_blocks_alone cover the same two passes for pinned blocks. tests/writable_session.rs::real_unsent_changes_survive_disabling_and_refuse_removal writes through a writable mount with uploads stalled, disables the account and reads the unsent payload back byte for byte, then asserts removal refuses and names what is at stake, leaves the journal where it was, and on an explicit discard moves the data aside rather than deleting it. Without the refusal it removes the account and its one unsent change.

rows.text: Disk-full recovery preserves edited data and explains required action.
rows.evidence:
Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. State as of 2026-09-10, rewritten for the same reason.
COVERED end to end. Preservation: a refused save leaves the sealed payload and the dirty working copy intact. Explanation: a full local budget and a physically full disk were both JournalError::Quota and both reached an application as ENOSPC, so a user was told 'no space left on device' on a filesystem with gigabytes free while the two remedies are opposite; DeviceFull is now separate and carries its own remedy. A real full ext4 showed that mapping was unreachable, because write_working persists metadata through SQLite before any byte and From<rusqlite::Error> discarded the reason. The daemon reports which of the two it was as AccountStatus.save_refusal. A writable mount now runs on a physically full filesystem, and the without-subject check showed the mapping decides what the KERNEL reports: without it an application gets EIO rather than ENOSPC.
STILL OPEN: no measured evidence on a real account for this row's own clauses. The live pinning run of 2026-09-11 covers pinning and offline reading, not the budget-filling, cleanup or disk-full behaviour these rows ask about.
rows.asserted_by: a_genuinely_full_filesystem_explains_what_to_free, which fills the filesystem it is given, asserts ENOSPC outside the journal before trusting any journal error, and fails against the previous code with 'it said: local upload storage is unavailable'. truncate_sparse_writes_and_quota_failures_preserve_the_working_copy and a_full_budget_and_a_full_disk_are_reported_as_different_problems still cover the budget half. real_a_refused_save_is_reported_as_a_budget_and_not_only_as_enospc drives a real mount into its budget through the kernel, asserts ENOSPC still reaches the application, asserts an earlier write was accepted so a wholly broken mount cannot pass it, and fails without the recorder. only_the_two_no_space_refusals_are_recorded_and_they_stay_distinct covers the classification, including that a non-space error leaves the field alone. STILL OPEN: no run has driven a mount on a physically full filesystem, so the device case is evidenced as a mapping and not as a journey. tests/writable_session.rs::real_a_save_on_a_full_device_is_reported_as_a_device_and_not_a_budget covers the device case through a writable kernel mount, with an accepted-before-full save so a mount that refuses everything cannot pass it. CI runs it on the same loop image as its journal-level sibling.

rows.text: Personal and business accounts, including multiple simultaneous accounts.
Explicit account, drive and SharePoint library selection.
Linked folders, duplicate links, moved/deleted links and folder-only access.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL, from work on other boxes 2026-09-09 rather than from a check aimed at this one (docs/validation.md#the-same-file-through-two-cold-mounts-with-the-path-off-and-on and #navigating-a-real-collection-while-it-is-being-indexed). The live account is itself an instance of this box: 42 nodes live in its own drive and 183,960 in a linked collection, reached through a single shortcut node whose target names the collection and its root item. Two consequences were measured rather than reasoned about. A fixture that builds its scope from account.drive.id addresses 0.02 percent of what is mounted and fails with 'remote item not found'. An engine given a root id that does not exist inside the named collection serves no listing at all and times out after two minutes without saying why; that now fails immediately with 'root item is not reachable in the named collection'. NOT COVERED: duplicate links, moved or deleted links, and folder-only access, none of which this account exercises.

rows.text: Per-item capabilities, restricted permissions and revoked-access behavior.
Remote creates, edits, moves and deletions update mounted views correctly.
rows.evidence: MOSTLY DONE 2026-09-09 (docs/validation.md#a-mounted-view-following-remote-creates-moves-and-deletions, and #catch-up-after-a-reconnection-and-the-periodic-recovery-refresh). Through a real read-only mount of an isolated account: a remote folder creation became visible in 5,058 ms, a rename in 4,654 ms and a deletion in 4,254 ms, the rename asserted on both halves so that a view adding the new name while keeping the old one fails. All three land at the five-second activity revalidation interval because the fixture watches that directory; a directory nobody is looking at follows the same changes by reconnection catch-up in 408 ms or by the thirty-second poll in 29,421 ms, each measured with the other disabled. rows.text: Defined filename, package/notebook, trash and unsupported-operation behavior.
Documented compatibility matrix backed by real-account checks.
GTK4/libadwaita setup and settings without a terminal in ordinary flows.
Account picker, mount controls, reconnect, connection removal and cleanup.
Tray status and actions using the daemon as the source of truth.
Nautilus badges, pin/unpin actions and consistent status refresh.
Actionable errors, progress, cancellation and conflict resolution.
Keyboard navigation, accessibility, localization and visual verification.

Verify a declared session matrix covering native Wayland and X11, and GNOME and KDE Plasma: windows, dialogs, system dark-style preference and portal-backed folder opening, including cancellation and missing-portal behavior. Record the actual backend and supported session combinations; Xwayland is not native Wayland coverage. Current CI uses Xvfb (X11) only and does not exercise a complete GNOME or Plasma session.

One application identity across the desktop entry, installed application icon, AppStream metainfo, desktop application's D-Bus name and Wayland `app_id`. Verify launcher/window association, including X11, on every declared shell; naming consistency alone is not a runtime check.

Install application-specific scalable and symbolic icons in standard theme locations, replacing the generic application icon. Check dock, launcher and software-centre presentation, including symbolic recoloring.
Implement the tray as StatusNotifierItem over D-Bus. Document the GNOME extension requirement, detect missing tray support and keep all actions available from the window when no tray host is present.

Publish a supported file-manager list beyond the initial Nautilus target, with an explicit Dolphin decision and a shared daemon status contract behind each integration. Unsupported managers must still access mounted files; badge/control availability must be explained.

Preserve actionable, sanitized error causes in the window. Unreadable or invalid settings, an unreachable service and an incompatible service remain distinguishable, with recovery actions and diagnostic detail appropriate to the failure. Never expose credentials or raw provider responses.
Native Arch/AUR, Debian/Ubuntu `.deb` and Fedora `.rpm` packages from the same release, with the clean-system checks in [Distribution](distribution.md).
Signed APT and COPR update channels, release artifacts, source/provenance, supported-version matrix and measured reproducible build procedure.
